newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan opposition urges support for Palestinians.
newsitem.headline: Jordan opposition urges support for Palestinians.

text.p: Jordan's Moslem-led opposition on Friday urged support for the "new Palestinian uprising" against Israel and demanded the government to freeze the 1994 peace treaty to protest against three days of violence.
The coalition of 10 political parties also asked Jordan to recall its ambassador to Israel, expell Israel's ambassador, Shimon Shamir, and halt normalisation of ties with the Jewish state.

Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti visited the "Palestinian" embassy in Amman earlier on Friday to convey Jordan's condolences to the families of 53 Palestinians who died in the fighting, sparked by Israel's opening of a tunnel close to a Moslem sanctuary in Jerusalem, officials said.
Headlines on front-pages of Jordan's state-controlled newspapers lambasted Israel, calling the confrontations a war and an intifada.

"We see the need to support the struggle of the Arab Palestinian people that ignited a new intifada (uprising) against injustice, the occupation and the Oslo (peace) agreement," they said in a statement faxed to Reuters.

"We urge the Jordanian people to declare their support to the Palestinian brethren and help them with all available means," said the group, led by the Islamic Action Front -- the single largest political party in the lower house of parliament.
"We ask the government to pull out the Jordanian ambassador from the usurper country (Israel) and to expell the ambassador of the enemy state from Amman."

King Hussein, whose country remains the historic guardian of Moslem holy sites in Arab Jerusalem since 1950, has been angered by the outbreak of the worst wave of violence since the 1993 Israel-PLO Oslo peace accords.
And so are many of Jordan's 4.2 million people who have family living in the West Bank, which Jordan ruled from 1952 until losing it to Israel in the 1967 Middle East War.

Amman says it will continue to have a role in Arab Jerusalem until the permanent status of the divided city is settled under the final stage of a Palestinian self-rule accord between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation.
Final status talks began in May but have been stalled since the election of Israel's hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu weeks later.
Jordan's treaty with Israel recognised Amman's "special role" over Moslem holy shrines in Arab Jerusalem -- a thorn in Jordanian-PLO ties.

King Hussein summoned ambassadors of the United States, Britain and Israel to his palace on Thursday night after returning from Qatar as part of a flurry of diplomatic activity to calm the violence and prevent possible regional tension.
He has asked Israel to close down the tunnel and demanded the formation of an international committee to probe the matter.
